concept_tested: Recall of the three ways in which ATP is formed by phosphorylation
stem: ATP is formed by phosphorylation, which is stated to occur in three ways. Which set names all three?

options.A: Photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
options.C: Substrate-level phosphorylation, oxidative phosphorylation and terminal oxidation

correct_answer_text: Photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation

distractor_rationale.B: Chemiosmosis is the name given to proton transfer across the inner mitochondrial membrane accompanied by ATP synthesis; it is not listed as a separate mode of phosphorylation.
distractor_rationale.C: Terminal oxidation is the step in which reduced oxygen combines with protons to give metabolic water; it is a step of aerobic respiration, not a mode of ATP formation.
distractor_rationale.D: Dehydrogenation is the removal of hydrogen from a respiratory material by dehydrogenases; no phosphate group is transferred to ADP in it.

solution: The three ways of forming ATP by phosphorylation are photophosphorylation, which occurs during photosynthesis, substrate-level phosphorylation, and oxidative phosphorylation.
formula_principle: ATP formation occurs by phosphorylation of ADP, and phosphorylation is of three kinds: photophosphorylation, substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
common_misconception: Students treat chemiosmosis or terminal oxidation as a fourth or a substitute mode of phosphorylation instead of as parts of the electron transport process.

concept_tested: Definition of substrate-level phosphorylation as distinct from the other modes
stem: Which statement correctly defines substrate-level phosphorylation?

options.A: Direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from a suitable substrate
options.B: Phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of NADH+H+ and FADH2
options.C: Phosphorylation of ADP using energy trapped during photosynthesis
options.D: Phosphorylation of glucose by transfer of a phosphate group from ATP

correct_answer_text: Direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from a suitable substrate

distractor_rationale.B: This is the definition of oxidative phosphorylation, in which the phosphate is not handed over by the substrate itself but is added using energy from coenzyme oxidation.
distractor_rationale.C: This describes photophosphorylation, the mode that operates in photosynthesis and not in respiration.
distractor_rationale.D: This is the hexokinase reaction of glycolysis; here the substrate is phosphorylated and ATP is consumed, which is the reverse of ATP formation.

solution: In substrate-level phosphorylation the phosphate group comes straight from a phosphorylated substrate and is handed to ADP, so ATP is formed without any coenzyme oxidation.
formula_principle: Substrate-level phosphorylation is defined as the direct phosphorylation of ADP by transfer of a phosphate group from any suitable substrate.
common_misconception: Students confuse the molecule being phosphorylated, thinking that any transfer of a phosphate group in the pathway counts as substrate-level phosphorylation even when it is glucose and not ADP that receives the phosphate.

concept_tested: Distinguishing the energy source and the site of oxidative phosphorylation from those of substrate-level phosphorylation
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes oxidative phosphorylation from substrate-level phosphorylation?

options.A: Oxidative phosphorylation uses energy released when NADH+H+ and FADH2 are oxidised, and occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.B: Oxidative phosphorylation transfers a phosphate group straight from a substrate to ADP, and occurs in the cytoplasm
options.C: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, while substrate-level phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.D: Oxidative phosphorylation adds a phosphate group to the respiratory substrate rather than to ADP

correct_answer_text: Oxidative phosphorylation uses energy released when NADH+H+ and FADH2 are oxidised, and occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane

distractor_rationale.B: The direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate is substrate-level phosphorylation; this option attaches that mechanism to the wrong mode.
distractor_rationale.C: The sites are interchanged; the matrix is the site of the Krebs cycle and the inner mitochondrial membrane carries oxidative phosphorylation.
distractor_rationale.D: In both modes it is ADP that receives the phosphate group; molecular oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor and does not phosphorylate the substrate.

solution: The defining features of oxidative phosphorylation are its energy source, the oxidation of the reduced coenzymes NADH+H+ and FADH2, and its location on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
formula_principle: Oxidative phosphorylation is phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of substrates like NADH+H+ and FADH2, and is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane; substrate-level phosphorylation is direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP.
common_misconception: Students remember that both modes make ATP but interchange the site, placing oxidative phosphorylation in the matrix alongside the Krebs cycle.

subtopic: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the balance sheet
concept_tested: Adding the substrate-level contributions of glycolysis and of two turns of the Krebs cycle
stem: In the aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, glycolysis yields 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and one GTP (ATP) is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation for every molecule of citric acid oxidised. One glucose gives two turns of the Krebs cycle. How many ATP molecules arise by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose?

distractor_rationale.A: This counts only the glycolytic contribution and omits the one GTP (ATP) formed in each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle.
distractor_rationale.B: This counts only the two turns of the Krebs cycle and omits the four ATP formed at the two ATP-yielding conversions of glycolysis.
distractor_rationale.D: 8 is the net benefit entered for glycolysis alone, which already includes the ATP credited to oxidative phosphorylation of the two NADH+H+.

solution: Glycolysis contributes 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle contributes 1, so 4 + 2 = 6 ATP arise by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose.
formula_principle: Total ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose = ATP from glycolysis (4) + one GTP (ATP) per turn of the Krebs cycle x 2 turns (2).
common_misconception: Students forget that one glucose drives two turns of the Krebs cycle and so credit only a single GTP (ATP) to the cycle, or ignore the cycle contribution altogether.

subtopic: Oxidative phosphorylation in the balance sheet
concept_tested: Converting the reduced coenzymes of one glucose into ATP using the accounting of the balance sheet and finding the gross total
stem: The balance sheet for ATP by aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule accounts each NADH+H+ as 3 ATP and each FADH2 as 2 ATP. Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose delivers 10 NADH+H+ and 2 FADH2 to the electron transport system, and substrate-level phosphorylation contributes 6 ATP. How many ATP come from oxidative phosphorylation, and what is the gross total?

distractor_rationale.A: This values only the NADH+H+ and leaves out the 2 FADH2, and it also mistakes the net figure for the gross total.
distractor_rationale.C: The oxidative contribution is right but 38 is the net figure obtained after subtracting the 2 ATP consumed in glycolysis, not the gross total.
distractor_rationale.D: This values every reduced coenzyme at 2 ATP, applying the FADH2 factor to NADH+H+ as well.

solution: The 10 NADH+H+ account for 10 x 3 = 30 ATP and the 2 FADH2 for 2 x 2 = 4 ATP, giving 34 by oxidative phosphorylation; adding the 6 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation gives a gross total of 40 ATP.
formula_principle: Oxidative phosphorylation ATP = (number of NADH+H+ x 3) + (number of FADH2 x 2); gross total = oxidative phosphorylation ATP + substrate-level phosphorylation ATP.
common_misconception: Students apply one conversion factor to both reduced coenzymes, or quote the net figure of the balance sheet when the gross total is asked for.
difficulty_basis: Extended synthesis across several claims, stages or calculations with high working-memory and trap density

subtopic: Identifying the mode of phosphorylation from the reaction
concept_tested: Recognising that an ATP-forming step inside the mitochondrion need not be oxidative phosphorylation
stem: Oxidative phosphorylation is defined as phosphorylation of ADP at the cost of energy released during oxidation of substrates like NADH+H+ and FADH2, and it is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane. In the Krebs cycle, which runs in the mitochondrial matrix, the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate yields one GTP (ATP). By which mode is that ATP formed?

distractor_rationale.A: The reaction is placed inside the mitochondrion, but no reduced coenzyme is oxidised on the inner membrane to drive it, so it does not meet the stated definition.
distractor_rationale.B: Photophosphorylation occurs during photosynthesis and has no role in any step of the Krebs cycle.
distractor_rationale.C: Chemiosmosis is the synthesis of ATP that accompanies the channelling of protons through the F0 part of the oxysome, which is not involved in this cycle step.

solution: In the succinyl-CoA to succinate conversion the phosphate group reaches the nucleotide directly from the substrate, so the ATP is formed by substrate-level phosphorylation even though the reaction takes place inside the mitochondrion.
formula_principle: The mode of ATP formation is decided by the mechanism of phosphate transfer, not by the compartment in which the reaction happens.
common_misconception: Students assume that every ATP made inside the mitochondrion must come from oxidative phosphorylation and that substrate-level phosphorylation is confined to the cytoplasm.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

stem: A tissue converts 5 molecules of glucose completely to pyruvic acid by glycolysis. Glycolysis consumes 2 ATP and produces 4 ATP per glucose. How many pyruvic acid molecules and how many net ATP molecules are formed?

distractor_rationale.C: This assumes one pyruvic acid per glucose, whereas the six-carbon sugar is split into two three-carbon products.
distractor_rationale.D: This adds the invested ATP to the output instead of subtracting it, giving 6 per glucose.

solution: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid and a net of 4 - 2 = 2 ATP, so 5 glucose molecules give 10 pyruvic acid and 10 net ATP.
formula_principle: Per glucose: pyruvic acid = 2, net ATP = 4 produced - 2 consumed = 2. Multiply each by the number of glucose molecules.
common_misconception: Students report the gross ATP figure as the net gain because they remember the four ATP of the pay-off phase more readily than the two-ATP investment.

options.B: A condensation by citrate synthase, giving citrate with release of CoA-SH
options.C: A decarboxylation giving acetaldehyde and CO2, with no coenzyme reduced

correct_answer_text: An oxidative decarboxylation by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, giving acetyl CoA, CO2 and NADH+H+

common_misconception: Students confuse the aerobic decarboxylation of pyruvate with the decarboxylation of pyruvate in alcoholic fermentation, which yields acetaldehyde and reduces no coenzyme.

stem: A cell-free preparation is supplied with glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate instead of glucose, and each molecule is carried through the remaining glycolytic reactions to pyruvic acid. Per glucose these reactions yield 4 ATP and 2 NADH+H+ from 2 such trioses. If 6 molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are supplied, how many ATP and NADH+H+ are formed, and how much ATP is invested?

options.A: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with 6 ATP invested
options.B: 6 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested
options.C: 24 ATP and 12 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested
options.D: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested

correct_answer_text: 12 ATP and 6 NADH+H+, with no ATP invested

options.B: Glucose is not completely oxidised, and the reduced coenzyme is spent on lactic acid or ethanol
options.C: Fewer glucose molecules are able to enter glycolysis when oxygen is absent, so fewer ATP are formed

stem: One glucose molecule yields two molecules of pyruvic acid, and each of them undergoes the connecting link reaction, producing one NADH+H+ each. distractor_rationale.A: This counts only one pyruvic acid; each glucose gives two pyruvic acid molecules, so the link reaction runs twice per glucose.
distractor_rationale.B: This counts the two NADH+H+ molecules themselves rather than converting each of them into 3 ATP.

stem: One turn of the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH+H+, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP counted as 1 ATP. Using the prescribed MHT-CET balance-sheet convention of 3 ATP per NADH+H+ and 2 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP are attributable to one turn?

concept_tested: Tracking the six carbon atoms of glucose into carbon dioxide
stem: One glucose molecule of six carbon atoms is split by glycolysis into two molecules of pyruvic acid of three carbon atoms each. Each pyruvic acid then loses one carbon as carbon dioxide in the connecting link reaction, and each of the two turns of the Krebs cycle releases two more molecules of carbon dioxide. stem: Rule: a pathway that oxidises its substrates stepwise, releases energy and gives off carbon dioxide is a catabolic pathway. options.B: It releases its energy in many small steps instead of all at once
options.C: It accepts substrates derived from carbohydrates, fats and proteins alike

concept_tested: Reasoning out why heavy withdrawal of intermediates limits the oxidative output of the cycle
stem: A cell is rapidly synthesising glutamic acid and aspartic acid, and so withdraws large amounts of alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate from the Krebs cycle. The supply of acetyl CoA to the cell is unchanged. Which statement best explains why the oxidative output of the cycle nevertheless falls?

options.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate carries the acetyl group through the cycle, so its removal leaves the acetyl group with no carrier
options.B: Both intermediates act as hydrogen acceptors at the oxidation steps, so their removal leaves the dehydrogenases without acceptors
options.C: Both intermediates supply the CoA-SH needed at the condensation step, so their removal blocks the formation of citrate
options.D: Oxaloacetate must be present at the start of each turn to accept acetyl CoA, so its removal limits the number of turns

correct_answer_text: Oxaloacetate must be present at the start of each turn to accept acetyl CoA, so its removal limits the number of turns

distractor_rationale.A: The acetyl group is carried into the cycle by coenzyme A and is handed to oxaloacetate at the condensation step; alpha-ketoglutarate has no such carrying role.
distractor_rationale.B: The hydrogen acceptors at those steps are NAD+ and FAD+, not the acids of the cycle themselves.

stem: In the balance sheet for ATP by aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, oxidative phosphorylation is credited with 3 ATP for each NADH+H+ oxidised and 2 ATP for each FADH2 oxidised. Using the same figures, how many ATP molecules would oxidative phosphorylation yield from 5 molecules of NADH+H+ and 2 molecules of FADH2?

distractor_rationale.A: This credits each FADH2 with 3 ATP, giving 15 plus 6; the balance sheet allows only 2 ATP for each FADH2.
distractor_rationale.B: This interchanges the two factors, taking 2 ATP for each NADH+H+ and 3 for each FADH2, giving 10 plus 6.

stem: For a completely oxidised carbohydrate the respiratory quotient is exactly 1, and for fats and proteins it is less than 1. One mode of respiration is an exception to this pattern of finite values. Which mode is it, and what is its respiratory quotient?

options.A: Anaerobic respiration, for which the respiratory quotient is infinity
options.B: Anaerobic respiration, for which the respiratory quotient is zero
options.C: Anaerobic respiration, for which the respiratory quotient is 1
options.D: Aerobic respiration on protein, for which the respiratory quotient is infinity

correct_answer_text: Anaerobic respiration, for which the respiratory quotient is infinity

distractor_rationale.B: Zero would require no carbon dioxide to be evolved; in fermentation carbon dioxide is evolved while no oxygen is taken up, so it is the denominator that vanishes.
distractor_rationale.C: A value of 1 needs equal volumes of the two gases, but no oxygen at all is consumed in anaerobic respiration.
distractor_rationale.D: Protein oxidised aerobically consumes oxygen and gives a finite value of about 0.9.

solution: In anaerobic respiration carbon dioxide is evolved without oxygen being consumed, so the denominator of the ratio is zero and the respiratory quotient is always infinity.
formula_principle: Exception to the finite RQ values: in anaerobic respiration CO2 is evolved without any O2 being taken up, so the denominator of the ratio is zero and RQ is always infinity.
common_misconception: Students see that oxygen is absent and set the respiratory quotient to zero, confusing a zero denominator with a zero numerator.

concept_tested: Calculation of RQ for the same tissue with and without oxygen available
stem: A tissue is studied twice. With oxygen freely available it releases 36 mL of carbon dioxide while consuming 40 mL of oxygen. Deprived of oxygen, the same tissue releases 12 mL of carbon dioxide and consumes no oxygen at all. What are the two respiratory quotients, in that order?

distractor_rationale.A: The second value is obtained by putting the zero oxygen figure in the numerator; the oxygen volume is the denominator, so the ratio grows without limit instead of vanishing.
distractor_rationale.B: The first value is misread as the fat figure; 36 divided by 40 is 0.9, the value the chapter gives for proteins.
distractor_rationale.C: A first value of 1 would need the two volumes to be equal, but 36 mL of carbon dioxide is less than 40 mL of oxygen.

solution: With oxygen available the ratio is 36 divided by 40, that is 0.9, the value given for proteins; without oxygen the denominator is zero while carbon dioxide is still evolved, so the ratio is infinity.
formula_principle: RQ = volume of CO2 released divided by volume of O2 consumed; when the oxygen consumed is zero the ratio is infinity, the value stated for anaerobic respiration.
common_misconception: Students apply the ratio mechanically and record zero for the oxygen-free case because the number zero appears in the data.

concept_tested: Benefit of a stepwise release of chemical bond energy during respiration
stem: Both anaerobic and aerobic respiration are conducted in many steps. What does a stepwise release of the chemical bond energy make possible?

options.A: The utilization of a relatively higher proportion of that energy in ATP synthesis
options.B: The utilization of the whole of the released energy in ATP synthesis without any loss
options.C: The release of that energy as heat rather than its utilization in ATP synthesis
options.D: The synthesis of ATP in the absence of any enzyme once the pathway has begun

correct_answer_text: The utilization of a relatively higher proportion of that energy in ATP synthesis

distractor_rationale.B: The claim made is that a relatively higher proportion of the energy is captured, not that the capture is complete.
distractor_rationale.C: The purpose of the graded release is to improve the capture of energy as ATP, not to divert it into heat.
distractor_rationale.D: Each of the many steps is catalysed by its own enzyme, and it is precisely the enzymes of those steps that allow the pathway to be regulated.

solution: Releasing the bond energy of the substrate in many small steps allows a relatively higher proportion of it to be used for ATP synthesis than a single large release would.
formula_principle: Utility of stepwise oxidation: a stepwise release of chemical bond energy allows a relatively higher proportion of that energy to be used in ATP synthesis.
common_misconception: Students overstate the claim and suppose that stepwise release lets the cell capture all the available energy.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Regulatory advantage arising from the many enzyme-catalysed steps of respiration
stem: The activities of the enzymes catalysing the different steps of respiration may be enhanced or inhibited by specific compounds. What does this make possible?

options.A: Control of the number of steps in the pathway according to the size and age of the cell
options.B: Control of the rate of the pathway and of the energy output according to the need of the cell
options.C: Operation of the pathway to completion without the formation of any intermediate compound
options.D: Maintenance of a constant rate of the pathway and energy output whatever the need of the cell

correct_answer_text: Control of the rate of the pathway and of the energy output according to the need of the cell

distractor_rationale.A: The steps of the pathway are fixed; what varies is the rate at which they proceed.
distractor_rationale.C: Intermediates are formed at every step, and some of them are drawn off for the synthesis of other biomolecules.
distractor_rationale.D: A constant rate is the opposite of what such regulation achieves, since the point of enhancing or inhibiting the enzymes is to match supply with demand.

solution: Each step of a many-stepped pathway is catalysed by its own enzyme, and since specific compounds can enhance or inhibit those enzymes, the rate of the pathway and the resulting energy output can be controlled according to the need of the cell.
formula_principle: Utility of stepwise oxidation: because each step has its own enzyme that can be enhanced or inhibited, the rate of the pathway and the energy output can be adjusted to the need of the cell.
common_misconception: Students regard respiration as a fixed automatic sequence and do not connect the multiplicity of enzymes with the possibility of regulating output.

concept_tested: Synthetic advantage arising from the intermediates of a many-stepped pathway
stem: A third purpose served by a many-stepped respiratory pathway concerns the compounds formed along the way. What is that purpose?

options.A: The same pathway supplies intermediates used in the synthesis of the molecular oxygen it consumes
options.B: The same pathway destroys its intermediates so that no other biomolecule can be built from them
options.C: The same pathway supplies intermediates whose only further use is the regeneration of the coenzymes
options.D: The same pathway supplies intermediates used in the synthesis of other biomolecules such as amino acids

correct_answer_text: The same pathway supplies intermediates used in the synthesis of other biomolecules such as amino acids

distractor_rationale.A: Molecular oxygen is consumed in respiration as the final electron acceptor and is not synthesised from any intermediate.
distractor_rationale.B: The intermediates are in fact drawn upon for synthesis, which is why the Krebs cycle is described as an amphibolic pathway.
distractor_rationale.C: Regeneration of the oxidised coenzymes is credited to the electron transport system, while the intermediates themselves act as precursors for synthesis.

solution: Because a many-stepped pathway generates a series of intermediates, those intermediates can be used for forming other biomolecules such as amino acids.
formula_principle: Utility of stepwise oxidation: the intermediates of the pathway can be withdrawn and used in the synthesis of other biomolecules such as amino acids.
common_misconception: Students treat respiration as purely catabolic and do not accept that a breakdown pathway also feeds synthesis.

concept_tested: Discrimination between the stated purposes of stepwise metabolism and a plausible non-purpose
stem: Four statements about a respiratory pathway with many steps are given. I: A stepwise release of chemical bond energy allows a relatively higher proportion of that energy to be used in ATP synthesis. II: The enzymes of the different steps can be enhanced or inhibited by specific compounds, so the rate of the pathway and the energy output can be controlled. III: The same pathway can supply intermediates used in the synthesis of other biomolecules such as amino acids. IV: The many steps allow the pathway to continue without enzymes once it has begun. Which statements are among the purposes served by such stepwise metabolism?

distractor_rationale.A: This omits the supply of intermediates for the synthesis of other biomolecules, which is one of the stated purposes.
distractor_rationale.B: This admits the claim that the pathway can run without enzymes, whereas each step needs its own enzyme, and it drops the improved capture of bond energy.
distractor_rationale.D: This admits the enzyme-free claim and drops the regulation of rate and energy output, which is one of the stated purposes.

solution: Better capture of the chemical bond energy as ATP, regulation of the rate and energy output through the enzymes of the individual steps, and supply of intermediates for the synthesis of other biomolecules are the purposes served; a pathway cannot proceed without its enzymes, since it is those enzymes that make regulation possible.
formula_principle: The three stated purposes of stepwise metabolism are better capture of bond energy as ATP, regulation of pathway rate and energy output through the enzymes of the individual steps, and provision of intermediates for biosynthesis.
common_misconception: Students read the many steps as a self-sustaining chain reaction and accept the claim that the pathway can carry on once started without enzymes.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

options.A: Building blocks for the synthesis of complex compounds are provided by the metabolic water of terminal oxidation

options.C: Building blocks for the synthesis of complex compounds are provided by the intermediates of the Krebs cycle

concept_tested: Calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient
stem: A respiring tissue consumes 50 ml of oxygen and releases 35 ml of carbon dioxide in the same interval. What is its respiratory quotient and the most likely main substrate?

distractor_rationale.A: 1.0; carbohydrate is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: 0.5; organic acid is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: 1.3; protein is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required calculating and interpreting respiratory quotient and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: RQ = carbon dioxide released divided by oxygen consumed = 35/50 = 0.7. A value near 0.7 is characteristic of fat as the main respiratory substrate.
formula_principle: Respiratory quotient equals volume of carbon dioxide evolved divided by volume of oxygen consumed.
common_misconception: The ratio is inverted or the carbohydrate value of 1.0 is chosen automatically.

concept_tested: Combining gas exchange from two respiratory substrates
stem: Two substrates each consume 100 ml of oxygen. Substrate P has an RQ of 1.0 and substrate Q has an RQ of 0.7. If they are oxidised together, what is the combined RQ?

distractor_rationale.A: 0.35 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gas exchange from two respiratory substrates and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: 0.70 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gas exchange from two respiratory substrates and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: 1.70 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gas exchange from two respiratory substrates and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: P releases 100 ml carbon dioxide and Q releases 70 ml. Combined RQ = (100 + 70)/(100 + 100) = 170/200 = 0.85.
formula_principle: For mixed substrates, add total carbon dioxide and total oxygen before taking the ratio.
